| [LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md) | Relational Frame Theory: Some Implications for Understanding and Treating Human Psychopathology | Barnes-Holmes, Barnes-Holmes, McHugh & Hayes (2004), International Journal of Psychology and Psychological Therapy 4(2):355–375. RFT stated briefly: humans relate events bidirectionally and arbitrarily, as a generalized operant under contextual control, so words take on the functions of what they are related to. Humans, unlike the animals of conditioning research, relate events bidirectionally, so a word acquires the functions of what it names. Relating is a generalized operant learned across exemplars, and its frames share mutual entailment, combinatorial entailment and the transformation of function. | [LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md) | Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control | Daw, Niv & Dayan (2005), Nature Neuroscience 8(12):1704-1711. Habitual and goal-directed control are model-free ("caching") and model-based ("tree-search") reinforcement learners in dorsolateral striatum and prefrontal cortex. Behaviour follows whichever controller's value estimate is less uncertain under approximate Bayesian versions of each. Simulations reproduce the devaluation data: over-training yields devaluation-insensitive habit, except for actions near reward or in tasks with more actions and outcomes. Both controllers serve the same ends; neither is the "irrational" one. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-459](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-459.md)), supplementary methods not read. Worth reading as the founding statement of model-based versus model-free control as two brain systems, and of arbitration between them by relative uncertainty. Goal-directed (devaluation-sensitive) behaviour is a prefrontal "tree-search" controller, statistically efficient but noisy to compute. Habit is a dorsolateral-striatal "caching" controller, cheap but data-hungry and blind to revaluation. Each controls behaviour when its value estimate is the more certain, which reproduces why over-training produces habits unless the task is complex or the action near the reward. Both controllers pursue "identical rational ends": a rejection of the impulsive-limbic-versus-rational-prefrontal picture. |
| [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md) | Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations: A reinforcement learning perspective | Botvinick, Niv & Barto (2009), Cognition 113(3):262-280. Hierarchical RL groups actions into reusable "options" with their own policies, subgoals and pseudo-reward. That eases the scaling problem by cutting the number of decisions to explore and learn. The paper builds an actor-critic version and maps option identifiers to DLPFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and option-length prediction errors to OFC. Unsuitable options produce negative transfer, so how useful options are discovered is the central open problem. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md)), from the PubMed Central author manuscript; the online appendix with the equations was not read. Worth reading as the bridge between hierarchical reinforcement learning (temporally abstract "options") and the psychology and neuroscience of hierarchically organized behaviour. Options ease the scaling problem of RL by shrinking search and learning to a few decision points. An actor-critic version maps option identifiers to dorsolateral PFC, option-specific policies to dorsolateral striatum, and option-specific values and extended prediction errors to orbitofrontal cortex. The problem it puts first is option discovery: the wrong options cause negative transfer, as in human problem solving. |

Worth reading as the argument that Pavlovian prediction, usually modelled as purely model-free, is also model-based. In the "Dead Sea salt" experiment a lever that had predicted a disgusting salt solution became, on first presentation after a novel sodium appetite was induced and before any salt was retasted, nearly as attractive as a sucrose lever, with mesolimbic activation. A cached value cannot do that. The CS must predict the outcome's identity, and its value must be recomputed against the current bodily state. The paper adds "defocusing" of outcome representations as a model-based route to apparent habit, and argues that dopamine can carry model-based evaluations. |
| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

| [LIT-1434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1434.md) | The power of goal-directed processes in the causation of emotional and other actions | Moors, Boddez & De Houwer (2017), Emotion Review 9(4):310–318. Standard dual-process models make stimulus-driven processes the default and give goal-directed ones a late, regulatory role, in action research and in emotion research alike. The authors reverse the default. Goal-directed processes, which select the action option with the highest expected utility, can be fast and automatic too, so most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, settled by the values and expectancies of outcomes. Emotional action tendencies can be caused this way. Appraisal-to-action-tendency links are sophisticated stimulus-driven processes. Evidence for stimulus-driven control rests on null results open to hidden goals. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1117.md)): in full, from the submitted manuscript deposited in Ghent University's repository. Worth reading as the shortest statement of Moors's goal-directed account of emotional action, and as the nearest prior statement of the record's reading of appraisal as negotiation. Goal-directed processes, which weigh the utility of action options by the values and expectancies of their outcomes, are the default cause of action, emotional action included. Most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, and its winner is fixed by values and expectancies. Control precedence is what high goal relevance produces, so an emotional episode is a decision process with higher stakes. The competition is run on a common currency, expected utility, which is the point where the record parts from it. |
| [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md) | Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | Berridge & Robinson (2016), American Psychologist 71(8):670–679. 'Wanting' (incentive salience, mesolimbic and dopamine-related) and 'liking' (hedonic impact, small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots) are dissociable. Repeated, especially intermittent high-dose, drug use can sensitize the 'wanting' system, making it hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, lastingly and perhaps permanently, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow during abstinence. Its scope is said to extend, on emerging evidence, to behavioural addictions and to the compulsions of dopamine dysregulation syndrome. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5171207, NIHMS816820). Worth reading as the authors' own short statement, a quarter-century on, of the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Drugs, and perhaps unpredictable non-drug rewards, can make mesolimbic 'wanting' systems lastingly hyper-reactive to cues and contexts, and 'liking' need not rise with it. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose a person's cognitive desire, operate without report, persist for years and grow during abstinence. It is a review of the authors' programme. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy for maintenance is valence, and the form addiction and metric fixation share ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), to which it gives a mechanism on the personal side. |
| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |
| [LIT-1476](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1476.md) v3 | Active inference and learning | Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, O'Doherty & Pezzulo (2016). An active inference account of choice and learning, on how goal-directed and habitual behaviour contextualise each other. Habits emerge naturally from sequential policy optimisation in agents equipped with state-action policies, as learned prior beliefs over policies; epistemic, ambiguity-resolving behaviour enables pragmatic behaviour and then habit. The important distinction is between belief-free and belief-based schemes, not model-free and model-based; the scheme covers dopamine transfer, reversal learning, habit formation and devaluation, and reduces to a Bellman scheme without ambiguity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1138.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading as the active inference account in which a habit is one more policy, its transitions and prior probability learned by counting the agent's own behaviour, so that habits form from goal-directed choice and, once formed, survive devaluation. It gives the record a published analogue of a learned log prior beside a precision-weighted evaluation. Simulation of one T-maze task only; its learned prior grows by frequency, not by reward, its reaction times are simulation run times, and the authors concede that it makes probably no new behavioural predictions. |
| [LIT-1477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1477.md) v3 | A systematic review of human avoidance learning: Cognition, computation, and methods | Mancinelli & Bach (2026; preprint 2025). A systematic review of 116 studies of avoidance learning in healthy humans with primary reinforcers, analysed for the phenomena a theory must explain and their power to tell theories apart. The evidence contradicts two-factor and other associative theories and favours expectancy and inference-based accounts, though residual avoidance after the outcome is visibly removed contradicts a purely inferential one. An available avoidance response protects threat expectancy from extinction, more so the more effective it is. The common paradigms are simpler than real-world avoidance, so tasks with larger computational demands and more action options are needed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1134](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1134.md)) from the PsyArXiv preprint, not the closed version of record; worth reading as the only systematic map of human avoidance learning, and for the finding, rated robust, that an available avoidance response protects threat expectancy from extinction, the more so the more effective it is. Avoidance is learned without ending the warning signal and transfers by inference, against two-factor theory; but some avoidance survives visible removal of the outcome, against a purely inferential account. Healthy volunteers with shock or noise only; nothing here is about anxiety disorders. |
| [LIT-1479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1479.md) v3 | Anxiety as a disorder of uncertainty: implications for understanding maladaptive anxiety, anxious avoidance, and exposure therapy | Brown, Price & Dombrovski (2023; preprint 2022). A narrative review and proposal, with no new data or model run. Cognitive-behavioural accounts put exaggerated threat expectancy behind maladaptive anxiety, but the learning literature (seven computational studies, chosen without a systematic search) fits better a disorder of uncertainty learning: altered adjustment of learning rate to noise and volatility, mostly for aversive outcomes. A narrative review and proposal: seven computational studies, chosen without a systematic search, show altered adjustment of learning rate to uncertainty, mostly for aversive outcomes; the avoidance loop and the account of exposure are argued in words and schematic figures, not modelled or tested. For fear-based disorders; by the authors' statement it does not explain GAD. |
| [LIT-1483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1483.md) v3 | The influence of anxiety on exploration: A review of computational modeling studies | Chou, Wilson & Smith (2024). A narrative review of computational modelling studies of how anxiety influences exploration, mostly in reward tasks and sub-clinical samples. In reinforcement-learning tasks directed, but not random, exploration may be raised by trait or cognitive anxiety and lowered by state or somatic anxiety; in foraging tasks anxiety is consistently associated with less exploration, including, in one study, less checking for a predator. Some differences may come from how anxiety modulates learning rates. Results are inconsistent and unreplicated, and tasks, anxiety measures and methods need to be made consistent. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1127](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1127.md)) from the CC BY PsyArXiv preprint, not the closed version of record, whose abstract differs; worth reading as the map of how anxiety relates to exploration once both are split into kinds. In reward bandits directed exploration tends to rise with trait or cognitive anxiety and fall with state or somatic anxiety, random exploration shows no link, and in foraging, and in one task with a predator to check for, anxiety goes with less exploration. A narrative review of mostly sub-clinical, unreplicated studies with inconsistent tasks and measures. |
| [LIT-1490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1490.md) v3 | Impaired action-safety learning and excessive relief during avoidance in patients with anxiety disorders | De Kleine, Hutschemaekers, Hendriks, Kampman, Papalini, Van Minnen & Vervliet (2023). In a computer-based avoidance task, 47 healthy controls were compared with 33 patients with OCD, 40 with panic disorder with agoraphobia and 66 with PTSD, before exposure treatment. OCD and PTSD patients avoided more during the safety cue and kept a higher expectancy of the aversive picture after the safety cue and after effective avoidance; PDA and PTSD patients reported more relief. The groups did not differ in avoiding the danger cues. The authors propose that low confidence in the safety that avoidance brings makes omissions surprising, and the extra relief reinforces avoidance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1123](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1123.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading as, by its own count, the third experimental study of avoidance learning in anxiety patients, and the first to track what they learn from avoiding as well as how often they avoid. Against 47 controls, OCD and PTSD patients avoided a safety cue more and, after effective avoidance, still expected the aversive picture more; PDA and PTSD patients reported more relief at omissions; nobody differed on the danger cues. Cross-sectional, with no cost to avoiding; relief was already higher before avoidance was possible, and patients rated the pictures as more aversive. That the excess relief reinforces avoidance is the authors' interpretation, not a finding. |
| [LIT-1494](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1494.md) v3 | Eligibility Traces and Plasticity on Behavioral Time Scales: Experimental Support of NeoHebbian Three-Factor Learning Rules | Gerstner, Lehmann, Liakoni, Corneil & Brea (2018). Behaviour unfolds over seconds and spikes over milliseconds, so learning rules must bridge the two. In neoHebbian three-factor rules, co-activation of pre- and postsynaptic neurons sets an eligibility trace at the synapse, which changes the weight only if a third factor (reward, punishment, surprise or novelty, carried by neuromodulators or special inputs) arrives while it is set. The review sets out four recent experiments supporting eligibility traces on the scale of seconds. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1130.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading as the review that set out what the first direct experiments (2014–2017) showed about eligibility traces on the scale of seconds: in striatum about 1 s, in cortex 3–10 s with the modulator setting the sign, in hippocampus about 2 s. Mostly slices, one laboratory per region, by theoreticians whose models assumed the traces; they grant that other mechanisms could bridge the same gap, and what is well established is the hour-scale tag of consolidation. |
| [LIT-1496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1496.md) v3 | Anxiety, Avoidance, and Sequential Evaluation | Zorowitz, Momennejad & Daw (2020; preprint 2019). A decision-theoretic analysis and reinforcement-learning simulations of maladaptive avoidance, with no data fitted. In sequential evaluation the chance to avoid danger later should make it less threatening now; a pessimistic false belief that one's own later avoidance will fail, with the danger represented correctly, propagates fear and avoidance to situations far before the threat. This one bias reproduces qualitatively exaggerated threat appraisal, fear generalization, persistent avoidance and laboratory findings on approach–avoid conflict and loss avoidance, and predicts a reduced free-choice premium in anxiety. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1136](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1136.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading for the derivation that avoidance far from a threat needs no overestimate of the threat, only an expectation that one will fail to avoid it later, which spreads threat value backward across a decision process. Simulations only, matched qualitatively to published findings (earlier cash-out, behavioural inhibition, aversive pruning); the predicted loss of the free-choice premium is untested, and the persistence of avoidance after the misbelief is corrected is argued, not simulated. |
| [LIT-1500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1500.md) v4 | Maximizing exposure therapy: An inhibitory learning approach | Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek & Vervliet (2014). A clinical translation of the inhibitory-learning model of extinction: the original threat association survives extinction, beside a competing inhibitory one, so fear can return; fear reduction during exposure does not predict outcome; and exposure should be designed to violate stated expectancies, not to reduce fear in session. Strategies: expectancy violation, deepened extinction, occasional reinforced extinction, removal of safety signals, variability, retrieval cues, multiple contexts and reconsolidation, with affect labeling as a further regulation strategy. Cognitive restructuring before exposure is held to blunt learning. Five illustrative cases; no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1137.md)) from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central, the accepted unedited version, not the closed version of record; worth reading as the standard clinical statement of the inhibitory-learning account of exposure: extinction adds a competing inhibitory association and leaves the original intact, fear reduction during exposure does not predict outcome, and exposure should be built to violate expectancies. It reports no data. Its strategies are cited to evidence of uneven strength, which the authors flag, and it reports the evidence against removing safety behaviours as well as for it. |
| [LIT-1505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1505.md) | Learning Through Reinforcement and Replicator Dynamics | Börgers & Sarin (1997; working paper 1993). For two players each running Cross's version of Bush–Mosteller learning with payoffs in (0, 1), the expected change of each player's mixed strategy equals the discrete replicator step of a two-population biological model, and in the continuous-time limit the learning process converges in probability to the continuous (Taylor) replicator dynamic at every finite time. Asymptotically it does not: the discrete process is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one for every learning speed. With negative payoffs the limit adds a probability-matching term to a replicator term in "benefits". | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md)) from the authors' working paper of October 1995, as held in Levine's Working Paper Archive; worth reading as the proved source of "Cross learning is the replicator dynamic": a single Bush–Mosteller learner with positive payoffs moves in expectation exactly as a population under the discrete replicator dynamic, and in the continuous-time limit follows the continuous replicator dynamic on any finite horizon. Two limits matter as much as the result. Asymptotically the discrete learner is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one at every learning speed, even in matching pennies where the replicator dynamic cycles; and with negative payoffs a second force, probability matching, enters beside the replicator term. |
| [LIT-1846](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1846.md) | Experimental reductions of delay discounting and impulsive choice: A systematic review and meta-analysis | Rung & Madden (2018). A systematic review and category-wise meta-analysis of 92 papers that tried to reduce delay discounting or impulsive choice by non-pharmacological means, in humans and animals. Most kinds of manipulation reduced discounting (Q(9) = 224.68, I² = 64%). Learning-based procedures such as bundling and delay fading gave the largest and longest-lasting effects. Framing and priming moved one-off choices. Clinical interventions moved discounting little: mindfulness and ACT (two studies) only at trend level, g = 0.32, p = .06. Formal mediation analyses were rare, so how any of these manipulations works is largely unknown. | Active — read in part 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1440](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1440.md), Skimmed) from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC6112163, NIHMS963171), fetched as PMC XML through NCBI's E-utilities after the PMC web page put up a reCAPTCHA; worth reading as the systematic review and meta-analysis of 92 papers on reducing delay discounting by non-drug manipulations, and for its finding that mindfulness and ACT moved discounting only at trend level. Read it knowing that effect sizes are pooled only within categories, that publication bias was not assessed, and that its search ended on 1 March 2016. |
| [LIT-2007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2007.md) | Human EEG Uncovers Latent Generalizable Rule Structure during Learning | Collins, Cavanagh & Frank (2014). EEG recorded during the structure-transfer task of Collins and Frank (2013), in that paper's Experiment 2 participants (N = 35), over three blocks. Each participant's context dimension was read online from reaction-time switch-costs. A late cue-locked negativity over right lateral prefrontal cortex was larger for switches of that dimension than for stays, with no effect for the other dimension, but did not predict transfer. An early switch positivity, absent at group level, and a classifier trained on a separate attention localizer, which decoded attention to each participant's context dimension, each correlated across participants with later positive transfer (ρ = 0.5 and ρ = 0.35); the two agreed only marginally. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1550.md)) from the publisher's typeset PDF posted on the first author's lab publications page; worth reading as the neural follow-up to Collins and Frank (2013), [LIT-2012](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2012.md), and as a worked case of corroborating a latent, individually built rule structure with several observables at once. It re-analyses that paper's Experiment 2 participants (N = 35), so it is not an independent sample; the late lateral-prefrontal switch negativity tracked each participant's context dimension but did not predict transfer, the early positivity that did was absent at group level, the two predictive markers agree only marginally, several topographic tests are uncorrected, and every contrast rests on a reaction-time switch-cost assignment. |
| [LIT-2011](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2011.md) | Context, learning, and extinction | Gershman, Blei & Niv (2010). Recasts Redish et al.'s (2007) state-classification account of renewal as Bayesian inference. Each conditioning trial (reinforcement, cue, context) is assumed generated by one latent cause, drawn from a Chinese restaurant process prior that admits an unbounded number of causes; inference over the assignment of trials to causes is run online by a particle filter, and responding follows the predicted probability of reinforcement. Simulations reproduce acquisition and extinction, ABA and ABC renewal and the context-dependence of latent inhibition, which Redish et al.'s model mispredicts, and with the concentration set to zero, so that no new cause can be inferred, the loss of context-dependence after hippocampal lesions and in young rats. Qualitative fits to replotted data. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1547.md)) from the APA version of record posted on the Gershman lab's publications page; worth reading as the normative, nonparametric account of why extinction does not erase conditioning: trials are assigned to latent causes under a Chinese restaurant process prior, so extinction is learned as a new cause and renewal and the context-dependence of latent inhibition follow, and setting the concentration to zero (no new causes) reproduces the effects of hippocampal lesions and immaturity. Its limits: qualitative simulations set beside data replotted from other studies, with no parameters fitted and no quantitative comparison; a static mixture with no representation of time, so no spontaneous recovery; no partial-reinforcement extinction effect; the lesion and developmental accounts rest on the one manipulation chosen to produce them. |
| [LIT-2012](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2012.md) | Cognitive control over learning: Creating, clustering, and generalizing task-set structure | Collins & Frank (2013). People learning stimulus–action rules by reinforcement may also learn which abstract rule, or task-set, a context signals. The context–task-set (C-TS) model clusters contexts onto latent task-sets under a Chinese-restaurant-process prior, reusing a task-set in proportion to its popularity or creating a new one, but approximates rather than performs the inference, keeping one task-set assignment per trial. A two-loop corticostriatal network that learns by reinforcement alone behaves like it, and its parameters map onto the model's. In two experiments where flat learning is as good as structured during acquisition, a new context signalling an old task-set was learned faster (positive transfer), and a new context needing a partly overlapping rule drew errors correct under an old task-set (negative transfer), significant over the whole group in Experiment 1, a trend in Experiment 2. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1545.md)) from the publisher's typeset PDF posted on the first author's lab publications page; worth reading as the paper that carries Chinese-restaurant-process clustering from category learning into task-set learning, with a model, a corticostriatal network mapped onto it and a transfer paradigm that measures structure people build without being asked to. The model is an approximate learner, not Bayesian inference; positive transfer replicated in both experiments (N = 33 and N = 35) but is modest, negative transfer reached significance over the whole group only in Experiment 1, the model-fit differences are "small", and each subject's structure is read from a reaction-time switch-cost proxy. |
| [LIT-2015](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2015.md) | Uncertainty in perception and the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter | Mathys, Lomakina, Daunizeau, Iglesias, Brodersen, Friston & Stephan (2014). Generalizes the model of [LIT-2016](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2016.md) to any number of levels and names it the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter: each level a Gaussian random walk with variance exp(κ x + ω) of the level above, scaled by the time between inputs. Variational inversion gives updates of one form at every level above the first, each mean update a prediction error weighted by a ratio of precisions: a value prediction error at level 1, a volatility prediction error above. Joined to a response model, it gives per-subject MAP estimates in transformed parameter spaces. Shown on two simulated agents differing in sensory uncertainty, one subject from Iglesias et al. (2013) with two response models compared by free energy, and a simulation study comparing four estimation methods at recovering κ and decision noise ζ. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1548.md)) from the open-access text in Europe PMC (PMC4237059); worth reading as the reference statement of the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter: n levels of coupled Gaussian random walks, updates that are precision-weighted prediction errors at every level (value prediction errors at the first, volatility prediction errors above), a perceptual model joined to a response model for per-subject MAP estimation, and a first simulation study of parameter recovery. Its empirical content is one subject and simulations; recovery was tested for two parameters of one model on one input sequence; κ and the prior on x3 are confounded unless one is fixed; and the scheme still assumes near-quadratic variational energies. |
| [LIT-2016](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2016.md) | A Bayesian foundation for individual learning under uncertainty | Mathys, Daunizeau, Friston & Stephan (2011). A generative model of an agent's learning: a binary state, a tendency whose logistic gives its probability, and a log-volatility, each level above the first a Gaussian random walk whose variance is exp(κx3 + ω) of the level above, the top one with constant variance ϑ. A mean-field variational approximation, with each variational energy expanded to second order at the previous posterior mean, gives closed-form one-step updates of Rescorla–Wagner form, whose level-2 learning rate is the posterior variance and rises with the volatility estimate. The parameters κ, ω and ϑ are fixed per agent, so individual differences are priors and each agent is optimal by its own lights. Simulations of 320 binary trials, perceptual uncertainty and a currency series illustrate it; mappings to anxiety and dopamine are speculative. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1552](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1552.md)) from the open-access text in Europe PMC (PMC3096853); worth reading as the derivation of what the later paper names the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter: closed-form, trial-by-trial updates for a hierarchy of Gaussian random walks in which each level sets the step size of the one below, so that the learning rate is set by inferred volatility and individual differences are fixed coupling parameters. Purely theoretical, as the authors say: simulations and one currency series, no data from people, no fitting, and no check of the variational approximation against exact inversion, which can fail when the variational energies are far from quadratic. |
| [LIT-2017](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2017.md) | Learning overhypotheses with hierarchical Bayesian models | Kemp, Perfors & Tenenbaum (2007). Learning needs overhypotheses, constraints on the hypotheses a learner considers; some must be innate, but a hierarchical Bayesian model can learn others while it learns the categories they constrain. In a Dirichlet-multinomial model of Goodman's bags of marbles, each category's feature distribution sits under two higher-level parameters, the within-category variability α and the population distribution β of each feature. Learned from a few labelled exemplars, low α for shape gives the shape bias, including generalization to a novel category from one exemplar, which matches Smith et al.'s (2002) training data qualitatively; the model also covers Nisbett et al.'s Barratos judgments, which a fixed-prior model does not. A Chinese-restaurant prior over kinds of categories discovers objects and substances, each with its own variability. Two stated predictions: two exemplars per category teach the bias best, and the abstract level can be learned faster than the concrete one. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1544.md)) from the version of record posted on the first author's site; worth reading as the paper that made learning an inductive constraint, Goodman's overhypothesis, a matter of inferring the higher-level parameters of a hierarchical Bayesian model, with the shape bias as its flagship case and a Chinese-restaurant extension that discovers ontological kinds. A computational-level modelling paper with no new experiments: its fits to published data are qualitative, the only rival fitted is a fixed-prior Bayesian model, the hierarchy and its top-level prior are given by hand, and the model does not account for Smith et al.'s no-name condition. |
| [LIT-2019](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2019.md) | Procedural Skills Decay in Emergency Medicine: A Scoping Review | Oskar, Prehoda, Sapp, Qi, Botticelli & Palaganas (2026), Cureus 18(3): e104804. A scoping review of procedural skill decay among emergency physicians: of 1349 records, 37 studies included (eight conference abstracts, six RCTs). Five themes: decay is seldom the primary outcome (30 of 37 used retention to evaluate a teaching intervention); follow-up is short (two studies beyond a year); few procedures are studied (ultrasound, CPR and airway dominate); assessment relies on simulation and checklists; few studies are of attending physicians (five). No decay rates, no quality appraisal. It ends with a call for longitudinal studies with decay as the primary outcome. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1612](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1612.md)) from the Europe PMC full text of the open-access version of record (PMC13051320); worth reading as a map of how little the emergency-medicine literature can say about procedural skill decay: of 37 included studies few make decay the primary outcome, two follow skills beyond a year, nearly all assess by simulation and checklist, few study attending physicians, and many required procedures are unstudied. Its main limits: descriptive counts only, no decay rates, no quality appraisal, 22% of included items conference abstracts, and a closing sentence on what decay depends on that the synthesis does not test. |
| [LIT-2079](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2079.md) v2 | A Meta-Analytic Investigation of Procedural Skill Retention and Decay | Tatel (2023), PhD dissertation, Georgia Institute of Technology, advised by Ackerman. A random-effects meta-regression of the change from acquisition to retention in procedural skills (learned actions with a non-verbal motor output), with retention interval in months as a continuous predictor: 1,281 independent-samples effect sizes from 425 of 457 sources. Decline is linear, 0.08 SD a month for accuracy and 0.06 for speed and mixed measures; about half of training gains are lost after 6–9 months (accuracy), 12–15 (speed) and 9–12 (mixed), and all after about 15, 27 and 30. Practice opportunities during the interval slowed decline for accuracy only. Residual heterogeneity is large and the moderators tentative; the author argues relearning during retention tests makes the estimates too low. | Active — read 2026-11-04 and 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1560, Read) from the PDF in Georgia Tech's institutional repository, the author's institution; worth reading as the precursor of Tatel & Ackerman (2025), [LIT-2088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2088.md), which stands unfetched, and as the most detailed account of its method: a meta-regression over 457 sources with retention interval as a continuous predictor, finding procedural skill declining linearly by 0.08 SD a month (accuracy) and 0.06 (speed and mixed), half of training gains lost within 6 to 15 months, and slower decline for accuracy when a performance opportunity, mostly an earlier retention test, fell in the interval. Its main limits: few long intervals (14 beyond a year), large residual heterogeneity, tentative moderators, and estimates the author thinks too low because of relearning and speed–accuracy confounds. Cite it, not the article, for results until the article is read. |
| [LIT-2088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2088.md) | Procedural skill retention and decay: A meta-analytic review | Tatel & Ackerman (2025), Psychological Bulletin 151(6). Unread; from the abstract, unverified until read. A random-effects meta-regression of the retention of procedural skills with motor components, with retention interval as a continuous predictor, over "1,344 effect sizes from 457 reports". The acquisition-to-retention difference grows by 0.08 SD a month for accuracy and 0.06 for speed and mixed measures; half of the gains made in training are lost after about 6.5 months (accuracy), 13 (speed) and 11 (mixed). Task type, complexity, intermittent performance opportunities and instructions are named as possible moderators, and relearning and speed–accuracy trade-offs as confounds. | Unfetched — filed 2026-11-04, not read. A lawful free copy is located and could not be fetched: Crossref carries APA's open-access licence and OpenAlex marks the work hybrid open access at the DOI, but the Crossref full-text link, https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/bul/151/6/696.pdf, answered on 2026-11-04 with HTTP 403 and an Imperva (Incapsula) WAF challenge page, and was not retried; no other APA host was tried. No PMC copy (Europe PMC has the abstract only, PMID 40455501), no PsyArXiv or OSF preprint found by title, and OpenAlex lists no repository copy. A human reader can likely open the APA copy. The first author's 2023 Georgia Tech dissertation, [LIT-2079](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2079.md), read in its results chapters, stands in for it: the same design, the same 457 sources and the same slopes, but 1,352 effect sizes against the article's 1,344, half-loss times given as three-month ranges where the article gives points, and nothing on what changed in peer review. It stays Unfetched until it is read, not on merit. |
| [LIT-2094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2094.md) | The Impact of Simulation-Based Spaced Training for Skills Acquisition on Learning and Performance Outcomes Among Healthcare Professionals: A Systematic Review | Patocka, Anderson, Brennan, Lacroix, Pandya, Ganshorn & Hall (2025; issue 2026), Simulation in Healthcare 21(4). Unread; from the abstract, unverified until read. A systematic review comparing spaced simulation training (several discrete sessions) with massed training (a single session) for skills acquisition in health professionals: of 4572 citations, 15 randomized or prospective comparative studies, of resuscitation and surgical procedures, mostly spaced about a week apart. Spaced training was generally as effective as massed, with some advantage for retention, particularly time to complete procedures, and no study showed effects on patient care or outcomes. | Unavailable — filed 2026-11-04, not read. No lawful full text found: OpenAlex marks it closed access with no repository copy; doi.org resolves to an abstract page at Ovid (https://www.ovid.com/jnls/simulationinhealthcare/abstract/10.1097/sih.0000000000000898~the-impact-of-simulation-based-spaced-training-for-skills), with the full text behind a subscription, and nothing further was tried there; it is not in PMC (PMID 41347740); a web search on the title and authors found no preprint, author manuscript or institutional copy. Only the abstract (Crossref, Europe PMC) was read. Martinengo et al. (2024), [LIT-2102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2102.md), read in full, is a neighbour, not a substitute: it shares the comparison of spaced and massed simulation for health professionals, but measures immediate post-training results, not retention, so it cannot stand in for this review's retention finding. It stays Unavailable until a copy is reached, not on merit. |
| [LIT-2102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2102.md) | Spaced Digital Education for Health Professionals: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis | Martinengo, Ng, Ng, Ang, Jabir, Kyaw & Tudor Car (2024), JMIR 26: e57760. A Cochrane-method review of 23 trials (3371 participants, 1990 to February 2023) of spaced digital education for health professionals: 17 of spaced online education, 6 of spaced digital simulation. Using immediate post-intervention results, spaced online education beat massed online education for knowledge (SMD 0.32, moderate certainty) and beat massed education or none for clinical behaviour change (SMD 0.67); spaced simulation beat massed simulation for skills in two studies (low certainty), with no significant difference in time to complete or errors. Most studies had unclear or high risk of bias, and none gave a rationale for its spacing interval. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1610](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1610.md)) from the Europe PMC full text of the CC BY version of record (PMC11502984); worth reading as a meta-analytic estimate of the spacing effect in digital health-professions education, separated by modality and by outcome level: a small advantage of spaced over massed online education for post-training knowledge (SMD 0.32, nine studies, moderate certainty), an advantage for clinical behaviour change, and a spaced-simulation advantage for skills that rests on two studies of low certainty. Its main limits: immediate post-training results only, not retention; mostly unclear or high risk of bias; and an abstract and body that disagree on the headline simulation effect (SMD 1.15 against 1.24). Registered as a neighbour of Patocka et al., [LIT-2094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2094.md), for which it stands in only partly. |
| [LIT-2222](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2222.md) | From Bainbridge to bedside: applying automation insights to medical curriculum and assignment design in the artificial intelligence era | Ahn (2025). A commentary that reads four points out of Bainbridge's "Ironies of automation" and pairs each with a remedy for medical education with large language models: deskilling by offloading, met by AI-free learning phases before AI is introduced; the monitoring trap, met by AI literacy and vigilance training; automation leaving the operator the complex and atypical cases, met by training for what AI cannot do; and the out-of-the-loop operator recalled at failure, met by simulations with injected AI failures. The ironies are Ahn's paraphrase of Bainbridge, with no quotation of her; the remedies are his. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1713](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1713.md)) from the CC BY-NC version of record in Europe PMC (PMC12683271); worth reading as the closest open restatement of Bainbridge's ironies of automation reached, mapped onto medical education with large language models, each paired with a remedy. A single-author commentary with no data; it paraphrases Bainbridge without quoting her or giving page references, so it shows how she is read, not what she wrote; its remedies are its own. |
| [LIT-2224](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2224.md) | Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers’ awareness? | Macnamara, Berber, Çavuşoğlu, Krupinski, Nallapareddy, Nelson, Smith, Wilson-Delfosse & Ray (2024). A theoretical perspective, with no data, arguing that AI assistants that take over cognitive work will accelerate skill decay in experts and hinder skill development in learners, outside the performers' awareness. Its premises come from automation research, chiefly aviation: skill decays with disuse, more for cognitive than physical tasks; disuse can be partial, a subtask ceased while the task goes on; in Casner et al.'s pilots, reported second-hand, procedural flying skills held while cognitive skills declined. It separates automation bias and complacency, which end when the automation is removed, from skill loss, which does not, and proposes research questions. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1710.md)) from the CC BY version of record in Europe PMC (PMC11239631); worth reading as a clear statement of how support that does part of a task wears down the operator's skill at that part while the task goes on, and why the loss stays hidden until the support is withdrawn. A theoretical perspective with no data of its own; its aviation evidence, chiefly Casner et al. (2014), is reported second-hand, without samples, sizes or horizons; and its claim that AI assistants accelerate decay beyond automation is a hypothesis it says no research has tested. |
